title: AI insurance: Exclusions operate beyond negligent hallucinations
desc: Shows policy wording, defence costs, aggregation and reporting can allocate AI risk independently of professional competence.

kps.k: Insurance terms can allocate AI-related legal risk independently of whether lawyers use AI competently.
kps.d: This cluster contrasts a contractual generative-AI exclusion with a regulatory minimum-coverage regime. Hamilton Select’s PL3026 endorsement expressly restricts coverage involving AI use; the SRA Minimum Terms and Conditions require broad civil-liability protection and permit only specified exclusions. These are contractual and regulatory evidence, not findings about AI error rates, claims frequency or market-wide insurance practices. They show different coverage structures rather than a direct disagreement about AI’s merits. The SRA terms govern a distinct regulatory setting in England and Wales; Hamilton’s policy requires claims to be brought in the United States, its territories or possessions, or Canada.

qs.q: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY  It is understood and agreed that Section III - EXCLUSIONS, is amended to include the following exclusion:   This Policy does not apply to any “claim”, “wrongful act”, “damages” or “defense costs” based upon, arising out of, or in  any way involving any actual or alleged use of "generative artificial intelligence" by the "insured".
qs.a: Hamilton Select Lawyers Professional Liability Policy with PL3026 Generative-AI Exclusion · Market & press · 2024

qs.q: Exclusions     The insurance must not exclude or limit the liability of the insurer except to the    extent that any claim or related defence costs arise from the matters set out in this    clause 6.
qs.a: SRA Minimum Terms and Conditions of Professional Indemnity Insurance · Regulators & courts · 2022

kps.k: Hamilton Select’s AI exclusion turns on actual or alleged use, not solely on hallucinations or negligent reliance.
kps.d: PL3026 reaches claims, wrongful acts, damages and defence costs involving an insured’s actual or alleged generative-AI use. It defines the technology broadly across content types and provides no express exception for human verification, supervision or accurate output. The practical implication is that checking AI output does not itself establish coverage under this wording. The endorsement demonstrates an express contractual restriction, but the supplied material provides no adjudicated interpretation, underwriting rationale or evidence of how often insurers impose or enforce comparable exclusions.

qs.q: As used in this endorsement, "generative artificial intelligence" means any type of artificial intelligence system that  generates or produces any form of content, including text, imagery, audio, media or synthetic data in response to training  data or user prompts, including but not limited to ChatGPT, Bard, Midjourney or Dall-E.
qs.a: Hamilton Select Lawyers Professional Liability Policy with PL3026 Generative-AI Exclusion · Market & press · 2024

kps.k: The SRA regime protects claimants while preserving limited insurer recourse against insureds.
kps.d: The SRA terms require cover for civil liability from private legal practice, prohibit avoidance or repudiation for disclosure failures and misrepresentation, and restrict denial for policy breaches. Insurers must direct indemnity payments to claimants without setting off debts owed by insureds, and must remedy qualifying unpaid excesses following claimant notice. These protections do not eliminate exclusions or reimbursement exposure: specified misconduct-related recovery must remain just and equitable, and dishonesty exclusions target responsible insureds while protecting others. Inconsistent policy provisions must be corrected or severed. The extracts contain no express AI assessment, so they do not establish that every AI-related loss receives cover.

qs.q: No adjustment or denial    The insurance must provide that the insurer is not entitled to reduce or deny its    liability under the insurance on any grounds whatsoever including, without limitation,    any breach of any term or condition of the insurance, except to the extent that one of    the exclusions contemplated by clause 6 applies.
qs.a: SRA Minimum Terms and Conditions of Professional Indemnity Insurance · Regulators & courts · 2022

kps.k: Defence-cost treatment and related-claim aggregation materially affect the protection behind headline limits.
kps.d: The SRA requires at least £3 million per claim for relevant recognised and licensed bodies and £2 million for other firms, excluding defence costs. Defence cover has no monetary cap, subject to a permitted proportional limitation when a claim exceeds the sum insured; the terms prohibit general aggregate limits. Hamilton Select instead counts defence spending against finite limits and ends its defence duty upon exhaustion. Both structures allow specified related claims to share a single claim limit. Firms therefore need to assess defence funding and aggregation, not simply compare nominal insured amounts.

qs.q: Any one claim The sum insured for any one claim (exclusive of defence costs) must    be, where the insured firm is a relevant recognised body or a relevant licensed    body (in respect of activities regulated by the SRA in accordance with the terms of    the body's licence) at least £3 million, and in all other cases, at least £2 million.
qs.a: SRA Minimum Terms and Conditions of Professional Indemnity Insurance · Regulators & courts · 2022

qs.q: The amount we will pay for “damages” or “defense costs” is limited to and shall reduce the applicable Limit of  Insurance.
qs.a: Hamilton Select Lawyers Professional Liability Policy with PL3026 Generative-AI Exclusion · Market & press · 2024

kps.k: AI coverage review must include ordinary exclusions, reporting duties and pricing—not just the AI endorsement.
kps.d: Hamilton Select separately excludes confidentiality and data-related exposures, fines and sanctions, and other specified liabilities. Its claims-made-and-reported conditions and prior-knowledge restrictions create additional coverage requirements. The SRA regime also permits specified exclusions, including fines and certain business liabilities, while preserving coverage through notification and continuity safeguards. It allows agreed risk-based premiums despite mandatory coverage protections. A practical implication is to distinguish civil damages, defence costs, sanctions, data incidents and contractual obligations, then check each against the applicable policy and regulatory requirements. Neither source establishes that AI has increased premiums or caused an insurance-market withdrawal.

vlens.an: This curated professional-voice evidence supports the cluster’s principal proposition through contractual policy wording rather than commentary, empirical risk analysis or a market-wide claim. The Hamilton Select endorsement allocates risk based on actual or alleged generative-AI use, so the exclusion is not confined to hallucinations, negligent reliance or failures of human verification. The policy also supports the proposition’s broader point that practical protection depends on ordinary insurance mechanics: defence costs reduce finite limits and the duty to defend ends when those limits are exhausted. Internal variation is therefore complementary rather than conflicting: one strand concerns whether an AI-related matter enters coverage at all, while another concerns how quickly otherwise applicable protection may be consumed. Because the record is a single policy and gives no underwriting rationale, adjudicated interpretation or evidence about other insurers, it cannot establish the prevalence of such exclusions or the insurance market’s general view of AI risk.

vlens.an: The regulator-authored source supports the proposition that insurance wording can allocate legal risk independently of lawyer competence or AI error. The SRA’s mandatory terms define coverage through broad civil-liability protection, tightly enumerated exclusions, separate defence-cost treatment, aggregation rules, claimant safeguards and limited insurer recourse. This makes the availability and extent of protection turn on the regulatory coverage architecture rather than solely on whether an underlying mistake involved negligent reliance on an AI hallucination. Material qualification comes from the source’s silence on AI: it neither evaluates AI-related risks nor establishes that every AI-related loss is covered. Its contribution is therefore structural and jurisdiction-specific—showing how the England and Wales minimum-terms regime constrains exclusions and defence-cost limits—rather than an express regulatory position on generative AI. Within that structure, protection is broad but not absolute: specified exclusions, aggregation and reimbursement rights remain available. Because the curated evidence here contains one regulatory instrument, it should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source supports the proposition at the level of insurance architecture rather than through an express analysis of AI. The SRA minimum terms show that coverage depends on mandatory policy wording governing permissible exclusions, defence costs, aggregation, claims notification, continuity and insurer recourse. That supports the proposition that legal risk associated with AI can be allocated independently of whether a lawyer acted competently or relied on a hallucination. Material variation exists within the regime: it combines broad civil-liability and claimant protections with enumerated exclusions, related-claim aggregation, proportionate limits in some high-value claims and reimbursement rights against insureds. Accordingly, it does not establish that every AI-related loss would be covered. Nor does it provide evidence about AI error rates, claim frequency or insurance-market practice generally; it is one regulatory instrument in England and Wales, and the curated source should not be treated as representative of insurers or regulators as a group.

elens.an: The supplied 2023–2024 source supports the proposition through contractual evidence that AI-related insurance exposure can be allocated independently of whether a lawyer acted competently. Hamilton Select’s endorsement excludes claims and defence costs involving actual or alleged generative-AI use; it is not limited to hallucinations, negligent reliance, or unverified output. The broader policy mechanics reinforce the proposition because defence costs consume the applicable limit and can terminate the duty to defend. Internal variation lies in the different mechanisms at work: the AI endorsement determines whether AI-linked matters fall outside coverage, while limits, aggregation, reporting conditions, and separate confidentiality or sanctions exclusions determine the scope and practical value of any remaining protection. This is one policy’s wording, not evidence of market-wide underwriting practice, claims frequency, or AI’s empirical risk.
